title: Guadalupe (1531)
hook: Catholics tell of Mary appearing to Juan Diego, an indigenous man, near Mexico City

segments.voice: Yesterday, Las Casas, the settler priest who gave up his laborers. Your line was they are our brothers.

A man takes the long way around a hill on purpose. His uncle is dying, he's running for a priest, and he doesn't want to be stopped. On this hill, the story goes, a lady has been speaking to him, sending him with messages to the bishop, and he has failed to bring back the sign the bishop wants. He's embarrassed and he's in a hurry. So he goes around. And she comes down the hill and meets him on the other path anyway.

This is the story Catholics tell of Our Lady of Guadalupe, told in one old account in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. Juan Diego is an indigenous convert living in the years just after the Spanish conquest of Mexico. On the hill of Tepeyac, near what is now Mexico City, a lady appears to him, speaks to him in his own language, and asks that a church be built there. He goes to the bishop. The bishop, cautious, asks for a sign. Then comes the uncle's illness, the detour, and the meeting on the other path. What she says there has become our line. In the story, she tells him not to be troubled or afraid, and asks: am I not here, I who am your mother? Are you not in my care? She tells him his uncle is already healed. Then she sends him up the hill to gather flowers, in a season when nothing should be blooming. He carries roses down in his cloak, his tilma, and opens it before the bishop. The roses tumble out, and on the cloth, the story says, is her image: a young woman with dark skin, in a mantle of stars, standing on the moon. Notice who the story honors. Not the bishop, not the conquerors. An indigenous man the powerful didn't believe. It sounds like Mary's own song in Luke: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree." The cloak hangs today in her basilica in Mexico City, and the Catholic Church honors Juan Diego as a saint. This is a Catholic devotion. Other Christians honor Mary in different ways, and some don't accept apparitions at all.

Remember someone with little power or money whose word you, or others, didn't take seriously at first: a child, a stranger, a worker, an elder. Hold what they actually said, and give it its full weight now. If you pray, you can pray for them, or with Mary's words from Luke, he hath put down the mighty from their seats.
Guadalupe. Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mary as Catholics tell of her appearing to Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, leaving her image on his cloak.
Your line: am I not here? Spoken to a man no one believed. That's nine hundred five.

howItsDone: Catholics in Mexico and beyond keep the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe with processions, songs and Mass, and pilgrims visit her basilica at Tepeyac to see the tilma.

chat.says: Who's the woman in the Guadalupe picture, and why does it matter so much?
options: Catholics say it's Mary, who came to Juan Diego, a man no one believed.
It's a Spanish queen whose portrait the conquerors hung in Mexico City.
It's the bishop's mother, painted to honor the church built on the hill.
chat.meaning: In the story Catholics tell, Mary appears to Juan Diego and leaves her image on his tilma. It honors an indigenous man the powerful didn't believe.

Nahuatl.meaning: Juan Diego's own language, spoken in central Mexico

Tepeyac.meaning: the hill near Mexico City where the story happens

tilma.meaning: Juan Diego's cloak, which carried the roses

Juan Diego.meaning: the indigenous convert in the story, honored as a saint

notes: Claims rule: the year in the index title is not repeated in the voice; 'in the years just after the Spanish conquest' is general. Confirm.
The Nican Mopohua is paraphrased throughout; the carry 'am I not here' is the index's rendering of the Nahuatl line; confirm.
Image description (dark skin, mantle of stars, standing on the moon): the tilma image's mantle is usually described as star-covered; confirm wording.
Historians debate the account's origins and dating; the script frames everything as 'the story Catholics tell' and does not adjudicate. A Keeper may want a note.
'Other Christians honor Mary in different ways, and some do not accept apparitions at all': confirm this is fair to Protestant and Orthodox listeners.
This is the broad Christianity path; Catholic devotion is described, not presented as shared by all.
